title: String to Integer (atoi)
description: Brute force to optimized: accumulating into a wider type and clamping at the end versus checking for overflow before every single digit.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Implement a function that converts a string s into a signed 32 bit integer, following the same rules a real number parser would: skip any leading whitespace, allow one optional plus or minus sign, read digits until a non digit character appears, and clamp the final result to fit within the signed 32 bit integer range.

blocks.text: Implement a function that converts a string s into a signed 32 bit integer, following the same rules a real number parser would: skip any leading whitespace, allow one optional plus or minus sign, read digits until a non digit character appears, and clamp the final result to fit within the signed 32 bit integer range.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Cashier Reading a Handwritten Amount
blocks.text: Picture a cashier reading a handwritten amount that might have extra spaces before it, an optional sign, and possibly some stray text after the number, like "42 dollars please". The cashier reads past the spaces, notes the sign if there is one, reads digits for as long as they make sense, and stops the moment something that is not a digit shows up.

blocks.caption: Skip whitespace, read an optional sign, read digits, then clamp to range

blocks.text: Since the parsed value would overflow the signed 32 bit integer range, the result is clamped to the maximum allowed value.
This problem sits right next to Reverse Integer in the sheet, and it is worth checking exactly how far that same overflow-safety idea carries over, and where the two problems genuinely differ.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Both problems parse digits and must guard against a signed 32 bit overflow, but this problem's input is a string that could contain any number of digit characters, not a value already bounded to 32 bits.

Observation 2: A tempting fix is to accumulate into a wider type, like a 64 bit integer, and clamp only once at the very end, but this only pushes the overflow boundary further away, it does not remove it, since a string with enough digit characters can eventually overflow even a 64 bit accumulator too.

Observation 3: Testing a concrete case, a string of eleven nines, shows the value actually exceeds the signed 32 bit range after only ten digits are read, well before the string ends, so continuing to accumulate the remaining characters is both unsafe and unnecessary.

Observation 4: The fix is to reuse Reverse Integer's exact same before-the-operation overflow check, applied one digit at a time, which stays correct no matter how many digit characters remain in the string.
That comparison, string of unbounded length versus already-bounded integer, is exactly what tells you a wider accumulator type is not actually a safe fix here, only a delay of the same problem.

Skip any leading whitespace, note an optional sign, and read every following digit into a wider type, like a 64 bit integer, so nothing overflows while the digits are still being read. Apply the sign, and only at the very end, clamp the result if it falls outside the signed 32 bit integer range.

items: Skip past any leading whitespace characters.
Read an optional plus or minus sign.
Read every following digit character, accumulating them into a wider integer type.
Apply the sign to the accumulated value.
Clamp the final value to the signed 32 bit integer range before returning it.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: accumulate into a wider type, then clamp only at the very end

codes.python:
import re

INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1
INT_MIN = -2**31

def my_atoi(s):
    s = s.lstrip()                                  # skip leading whitespace
    match = re.match(r'^[+-]?\d+', s)                 # grab a valid sign followed by digits, if any
    if not match:
        return 0                                       # no valid number found at the start
    value = int(match.group())                        # Python integers have no fixed width, so this is exact
    if value < INT_MIN:
        return INT_MIN                                   # clamp to the smallest allowed value
    if value > INT_MAX:
        return INT_MAX                                   # clamp to the largest allowed value
    return value


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "   -42"
    print(my_atoi(s))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Whitespace and the optional sign are each handled as their own small, self contained step, so the main digit reading loop can assume it starts exactly where the actual number begins.

The accumulator is deliberately a wider type than the final signed 32 bit result, giving the digits room to accumulate past the 32 bit boundary temporarily before the clamp step decides what to do about it.
The clamp check happens only once, after the loop, since this version is relying on the wider type to have safely held whatever value accumulated during the loop.

blocks.text: This correctly parses the number and clamps it, since using a wider type while reading the digits means the value being accumulated cannot silently wrap around before the final clamp check runs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass through the string.
Space: O(1) extra space beyond the accumulator itself.

Limitation: using a wider type only pushes the overflow problem to a larger boundary, it does not remove it. A string of enough digits, say thirty nines in a row, can still overflow even a 64 bit accumulator before the final clamp ever runs. The safe fix is to check for overflow after every single digit, using only ordinary 32 bit range arithmetic, and stop immediately the moment it would be exceeded.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the wider type version works for most inputs but is not truly safe: it assumes the input will never contain enough digit characters to overflow the wider accumulator, an assumption the problem does not actually guarantee.

What stays the same as Reverse Integer: the underlying technique, check whether the next multiply-and-add step would exceed the allowed range, before performing it.

What is different here: the input length itself is unbounded, so the check must run after every single digit, for as long as digits keep appearing, rather than just once for a value already known to fit in 32 bits.

Can the same rearranged overflow condition be reused directly: yes, result greater than INT_MAX minus digit, divided by 10, applies here exactly as it did for Reverse Integer.

The core idea: read digits one at a time, checking the overflow condition before every single addition, and stop and clamp immediately the moment it would be exceeded, regardless of how many digit characters remain.

Read digits one at a time, and before adding each new digit to the result, check whether doing so would push the result past the maximum allowed value. If it would, stop immediately and return the appropriate clamped boundary. This way the result is never allowed to exceed the signed 32 bit integer range at any point, no matter how many digit characters the input contains.
Read digits one at a time, checking before every single addition whether it would push the result out of range, and stop immediately with the correct clamped value the moment it would.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: check for overflow before adding every single digit

blocks.text: This works because the overflow condition, result greater than INT_MAX minus digit, divided by 10, is derived directly from rearranging the operation it is protecting, result times 10 plus digit greater than INT_MAX, solved for result. Checking this before every single digit, rather than once at the end, means the loop can stop the instant a genuine overflow is detected, regardless of how many more digit characters the string might still contain.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same order as the brute force, but with an early exit as soon as overflow is detected.
Space: O(1) extra space, and unlike the wider type version, this stays completely safe no matter how many digit characters the input contains, since the result is never allowed to grow past roughly the maximum allowed value at any point.

blocks.text: Parsing problems like this one are less about algorithmic complexity and more about carefully handling every edge case: whitespace, an optional sign, where digits stop, and what happens on overflow. Checking for overflow one digit at a time, rather than accumulating first and clamping later, is the only approach that stays correct no matter how long or extreme the input is.

items: Clamping only after fully accumulating the value, which can still overflow even a wide intermediate type on a long enough digit string.
Forgetting that only ONE leading sign character is allowed, and that a sign appearing after some digits have already been read should stop the parse instead.
Not stopping at the first non digit character, and instead trying to interpret the rest of the string.

blocks.text: This problem is really a checklist of edge cases in disguise, listing them out loud, whitespace, sign, digit stop, and both overflow directions, before writing any code shows a methodical approach that interviewers specifically look for on this exact problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "is a wider accumulator type enough", think: no, it only moves the overflow boundary further away, a per digit check is the only fully correct fix.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to Reverse Integer", think: the exact same before-the-operation overflow check, just applied to a string of unbounded length instead of an already-bounded integer.
If the interviewer says "what happens after a valid number ends", think: stop reading immediately at the first non digit character, ignore everything after it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(n) time, one pass through the string. The wider type version uses O(1) extra space but is only safe up to the width of its accumulator type, while the digit by digit overflow checked version also uses O(1) extra space but stays correct for a string of any length, the real floor for this problem.

items: Pattern: string parsing with a strict rule sequence, whitespace, then sign, then digits, then stop, combined with an overflow check that must stay correct no matter how many digit characters the input contains.

Core Idea: reuse Reverse Integer's before-the-operation overflow check, applied one digit at a time, since a wider accumulator type only delays overflow rather than removing it for an input of unbounded length.
Time: O(n) for both the brute force and the optimized version, with an early exit on overflow in the optimized one.
Space: O(1) extra for both versions, though only the optimized version stays correct regardless of input length.
Most Important Observation: widening an accumulator type is a false sense of safety when the input length itself is unbounded, only a genuine per step check is truly correct.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write a version that passes typical test cases; recognizing why the wider-type version is not actually correct for all inputs is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: same before-the-operation overflow check as Reverse Integer, just applied once per digit of a string with no length guarantee.
